projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charles Ginza was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II and Korean War veteran Charles A. Ginza. Mr. Ginza served in the U.S. Army Air Corps and later the Air Force. During World War II, he served stateside and in Panama. I'm Tom Swope (ph), and this recording was made at Mr. Ginza's home near Chardon, Ohio, on October 17th, 2003. Charles was 83 at the time of this recording. Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: I was living in Panama. I was already in the service.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, really. So when did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: I went into the service in January, 1940, just after I graduated high school. I looked around for some kind of work to do. And it was during the depression days, and you didn't find anything, you know. So everywhere you went, they asked you, well, how much experience do you have. I said, well, I have none, I just graduated high school, and I have a little experience in machine shop work, a little bit in carpentry, and so on. He says, well, when you get a little more experience, come back with us, to us. I says, well, yeah, I'm going to wait 20 years before I get more experience. So I decided, well, we used go to town every so often with a bunch of guys I used to hang out with -- well, actually, it was only one family. And every so often, we'd go to town, and I'd go by the post office in Buffalo, and there would be these stands, you know, where say join the Army, join the Navy, and join the Air Force, and so on and so on. So I says, well, I'm going to go into one of them places and see what they got to say. And I did.

And first of all, I went into the Navy, the recruiter there, you know. And he, we were talking, and he was satisfied with everything I could tell him, and I had my high school diploma and everything. And we went along pretty good until he says, well, how long is the enlistment. He says, oh, the enlistment, first year enlistment is a six-year enlistment. I says, yeah, well, if I don't like it, I'm going to have six years of hell, you know. I says, I'm going to just be, just go nuts. Anyway, I said I'll let you know. I went into, the next office I went to was the Air Force place. And he sounded like he was, you know, interested. They all do, you know. They all tell you the best high spots of all the service, you know, what they do.

And I says, you know, and I finally come to the question, well, how long is the Air Force enlistment. He says, oh, the Air Force enlistment is for three years. I says, well, that wasn't too bad, you know, I mean, if I don't like it, I could probably stick it out for three years. So anyway, he -- I decided to, I say, where would I put in or where would I be shipped to or what kind of assignment would I have. And he says, well, we could send you anywhere overseas you want to go.

And I says, well, what is overseas. He says, well, Hawaii, Panama, and he mentioned a few other. I says, Panama sounds okay. It's not too far, and yet, you know, it's overseas. So I went ahead, and I went home and told my parents, well, I was down to the recruiter, and I talked to him, and I think I'm going to go ahead and join the Air Force. Only at that time, it was the Army Air Corps.

And so the papers were made, were signed, and I passed the physical, and I passed everything, and the written test and so on, and wound up, after I signed up, I went through my basic training at Fort Slocum, which probably most people don't even know there was a Fort Slocum. It's near Jersey and New York Harbor in there somewhere where you have to go by ferry. So I had my basic training over there, and two, three months, and first thing I know, I was on a boat going to Panama.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Anything unusual happen during your basic training?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No, nothing unusual. They just taught us how to march, taught us which is the left foot and which is the right foot, (laughter) and you know, and I did some KP, and just nothing much at that time as far as basic training was concerned. It didn't have, like the Army, you know, you go out there in the field, you got a rifle and you shoot and all that. Air Force at that time wasn't that way. So, when I got to the, what I wanted, where I landed in Panama -- by the way, the name of the boat was, I still remember, was the Shadow Theory. It was, I don't know, I think, whether it was a passenger boat or whether it was just one of those merchants that carry supplies and everything else, you know. So I landed there, and then I was picked up by, you know, truck, one of those Army trucks, and wound up in France Field, was the name of the field on the Atlantic side, was France Field. So I spent about a year-and-a-half there, and then we heard, you know, the Japanese bombed Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the outfit down there in Panama?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Down there was, well, I first started out as a sweeper, sweep out the hangers. A lot of us were. Anyway, I wound up where I got interested in armament and gunnery and so on. So I was in the field. Towards the end, I was gunnery maintenance and gunnery training. Later on, came on that we were training other crews to go overseas, but that's getting ahead of myself. Anyway --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, what are your memories then? You just talked about Pearl Harbor. What are your memories of that day, of December 7th, 1941?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Well, what I remember of that was, we were all settled at France Field, and we were doing all our duties, our training and normal duties and so on, and we heard that Japan was bombed, and the commanders there got word or rumored or something that after the Japanese bombed Hawaii, they were going to be heading south, thinking, they was thinking that maybe they were going to try to knock out the Panama Canal. So what happened, we, people at France Field just packed everything up, planes, every piece of equipment they could find, and we went into a remote air field they had in the jungle.

And the name of that place was Ria Jara (ph). So there we were, we were sitting in, living in tents, and everything was just temporary, you might say. But it turned out that they were there longer than just temporary. And about that time, I was an armorer and gunner. I was on a B-17 or B-24. I was taking care of the guns and everything, ready, in condition to fire, you know. And they started sending crews from the states, you know, combat crews, B-17s and that. And we were training them how to shoot, how to take care of the machine guns, and how to take care of the planes, and how to take care of the armament and everything, and how to shoot.

They would take off and we had a plane that would throw targets, you know, and they would be shooting at that and see. We were a training base there for a while. And about that time we started doing all that, the war was getting pretty hot and heavy, and my enlistment was coming up to an end, you know.

So as it happened, they said, well, we can't let you out, they says, because you're -- everybody that was already in the service, he would go ahead and go for the duration. If it stay ten years, you were there ten years. Anyway, about that same time, my enlistment was winding up, and I was going to be reassigned. They probably were going to send me to the states in some outfit to be an aerial gunner or something.

So I decided, well, there was a notice on the bulletin board, and kind of caught my eye. I says, well, gee whiz, you know, the bulletin board said something about anybody interested in becoming an Air Force pilot should submit his name and everything, and he will be given a test and tested and everything to see if he will, if he's pilot material, you know. Well, about this time, I was what, 21, going on 22, 21, something like that, and I was in fairly good health and pretty good condition and everything, so I put in for it. Well, they send me into the states, and I had to, I think it was San Antonio, took all kinds of physical tests and all kinds of everything that a pilot goes through today to see how he can withstand all the different stresses, you know, and a written test.

I passed the written and everything, so I decided that, well, I'm going to go further on, you know. The next thing I hear was that we're going to send you -- by this time, they had the classes all made up. I was in 45C. And they had the classes already formed or the group of people that were going to be in the class go into training as one group. So they sent us notice that -- well, they didn't send a notice out, but they informed us that we're going to send you out through three months of college refresher course.

I says, well, that's the end of me. I never even went to college. I never saw college. But anyway, it turned out that it was a couple of college guys that were in that, in my group. In fact, most of them were. I was the only -- by that time, of course, I forgot to tell you, I was already a staff sergeant in the service as an enlisted man. And they were mostly interested in, of course, college graduates, not as much as they are today. So there was a couple guys that I got pretty friendly with, and they helped, they helped me breeze through the three years of refresher. I never had this stuff in high school. So I managed to scrape through that.

So from then on, things were getting easier because then you were actually getting into the flying phase of it, you know. So I had a little flying -- by the way, I went to Michigan State College. That's where they sent us for the 30 days, or 90-day, three-month course. And they had little Cubs there that they would take us up in planes and let us handle them, fly and all that. And they would go ahead and evaluate what, you know, what they found would be the false or good points, you know, in my -- in other words, they were checking me out to see if I would make a pilot, you know, further on down the line.

Well, it turned out that, yeah, I would make it -- just a minute. I have a little here. It shows my college -- excuse me -- my college training and some of the comments they made. And from there, after the 90-day period, my whole class, 45C, went down to Curtis Air Field in, in Brady, Texas.

And we stayed there, heck, I don't remember now how long it was. I think it must have been three or four months, you know. And that's where you learned the basics of flying. I mean, they have a -- well, at that particular time, he was a civilian pilot, but he was hired by the government to teach, you know, flying. And you had to, you had to solo in ten hours or less.

Well, I did that. I did go ahead and I turned out that I liked it, and it was a PT-13. It was one of these two-wing jobbies with the, it looked like wire cables holding the wings together so that, you know, they wouldn't fly off. It was open cockpit and not much of instruments. They had maybe altitude and speed, and that's about all they had, and a compass. And the radio system was you had a tube like, say, something like this, and he had a tube underneath tucked in his ear, and he could hear what I had to say, and I could hear what he said. Anyway, we were flying around there. He was teaching me. We were going through different maneuvers and different things that you would encounter in flying, and in fact, they would even take you up to about 5,000 feet or higher, and then they would put it into a stall and purposely go into a spin, you know, going down. So he did that a couple of times. He says, now, you do that. I says, okay, I'll give it a shot, you know. So I stall it out, and then I start going down. He says, pull out in about three turns. I says, well, I think I pulled out in three or four turns. And he says, well, that was good, you know, that part of it. I didn't like it though. I would never make a fighter pilot because it was too, too hectic, and I was, it was, you know, you had to be upside down, sideways, and all kinds of, you know, positions to fly and all. An airplane would be like rolling and all that stuff. So I didn't much care for the acrobatics is what I would call it. So anyway, I went through that all right. So now he said, we'll take off, and they had three or four air fields around the area where they used for landing and all, all set up for that. And I went ahead, and he says, he took me out to that one field. He says, well, I landed, you know, and everything.

And he says, well, pull over there to the end of the field, he says, and I says okay. And he got out. And I says, well, this is it. I said, you know, I either make it or break it. Well, I was fairly sure that I would be all right. Anyway, I took off. He says go around the field, take, you know, one time, and then make a landing. I says, okay. I took off, went around the field, and I came back down, and I made, of all the times that I landed the plane, that was the only time I made a three-point landing, I mean where the front wheels and the tail hit the ground at the same time. Most of the time you hit, when you come for a landing, you hit with your front wheels and then the tail goes down. Well, anyway, that was the only time that I ever made a three-point landing. He says, okay, that's fine. Now, fly me back to the regular base, you know, where they were, where most of the planes were sitting already.

And he got out there, and he says, now, you go up and take it up for about half an hour and play around by yourself. Boy, didn't I feel like I was King Tut, you know. Here I am flying around, you know, in this big flying machine, you know, all by myself.

I felt like a million bucks, you know. And well, I keep -- people tell me how did it feel like to be flying up by yourself. I said, well, think of it this way: If you remember the first time you drove your father's car or your first automobile that you bought and you passed the driver's test and everything, and he says, now, you go out by yourself. What kind of a feeling you had when here you were driving all by yourself, you know, and nobody to tell you where or how to go or what to do and someone, and you feel like, you know, you were somebody, and just triple that three times. That's what I felt like when I soloed in the little Stearman.

So anyway, from there, we finished our training, and we went from there to basic training. This was primary, the first phase, and the basic was the second phase. We went down to Black Rack (ph), I believe, is the name of that -- it was on the border of Texas and Mexico, and there was a little town right across the street. But anyway, this base was located on the state side. It was AT6s. And those were -- well, it was more of a sophisticated airplane. They even fly them around today. It had twice as much horsepower. It was a single wing with canopy and a full dash of instruments. And something new, of course, was landing gear, you had to remember, and you had flaps that you could move, operate and use when you needed to and so on. And that was the AT6 that today, when you see a Japanese zero when they show a movie, well, it's an AT6 only painted up to look like, you know, with the sun and everything on the tail. So an AT6 was a quite a jump from a PT-13 to this. This was -- the other one was about 150 horsepower, and this was or 400.

A lot more airplane, you know. I says, well, boy, I'll tell you, this is going to be something. So we went through, and there you learned how to rely on your instruments a little more. You had more, you had a full board of instruments. You had everything, radio. And you learned all the finer points of flying. Today, I don't know if they teach you that today or not, but they probably, you know, insert that in with other training. But this was a separate field or a separate branch like, field of training. And they taught you how to fly by instruments, and they tried -- what they did was to make you believe, teach you to believe those instruments. In other words, when that instrument says that your wing was low, you should, you know, straighten it because it would show that way on the instrument, showed that your plane wasn't straight and level.

Well, as time went on, towards the end there, they figured, well, this was about time to teach or show me or see what I can do with the hood covered up, you know, where you couldn't see outside, and all you had was the instruments in front of you to look at, you know, and see how you're flying and everything else. In other words, you were in the dark. The pilot was open. He was in the front cockpit. I was in the back. And that was the tough part. I didn't like to believe in them instruments. I want to see the ground. I want to see the eye, you know, with my eye, well, the ground is here, and I'm going this way or that way. I didn't trust them too much.

But I got through it somehow. I almost didn't because I didn't want to believe in those instruments, you know. But today, hey, they got to believe in them because of the weather they fly in, these commercial pilots. They go through storms and land in the night with storming and everything else, they have to believe in them. But I didn't want to. (Laughter.)

Anyway, we went through that phase, and we graduated. And from there, we went to Enid, Oklahoma. And while I was in Enid, Oklahoma, they introduced us to the B-25 which is an airplane that's about three times bigger than the AT6, two engines, and it's a medium bomber. You know what they look like, B-25? And I says, holy smokes, I'm going to learn how to -- I don't know if I'll be able to hack this, you know. But then we went out. I had an instructor pilot. We went up a few times and landed and so on and so forth, and he showed me, you know, the finer points of flying a B-25. And I kind of got through it okay. And towards the end of the training in a B-25, I liked to fly it better than I did the Six or the Stearman, you know. I mean, it was easier to handle, more responsive. You had a tricycle landing gear. You could land. I mean, it was a snap. It was easy. It was like driving a Model T and then getting into a Cadillac, you know. And I really liked it.

One time, I goofed up, though, me and another student pilot. We were, we left, and we were supposed to go to Enid, Oklahoma, to somewhere around Albuquerque, New Mexico. We went across country. And then we were supposed to come back and hit another point and then come back. Well, my co-pilot -- I wasn't watching too closely either. He didn't watch too closely. He was too busy looking outside look what's going on, so we missed our point to turn. And I says, hey, I think we should have, we should have found that, you know, spot on the ground or the city that we were supposed to go around and start head for home. And sure enough, we did miss it, and we were heading -- I says, well, now what do we do.

I says, well, let's call the Air Force. I looked at the maps. They told you how to read the maps and everything and the books and radio signals and everything, you know, how to contact other bases. And I, I noticed that we were heading towards San Antonio, you know, from Albuquerque, we were supposed to go, I was heading to San Antonio. And I says, this is Air Force so and so, so and so, so and so. We goofed up on our cross country, and we're running a little bit on low, and we ask permission to land at San Antonio. So they, of course, radioed back and they says, yes, of course you can.

And in the meantime, they send out the fire trucks and everything else just in case, you know. So like a pro, we went -- I went around, and later made a beautiful landing, and landed and everything like a professional that flew for 20 years, you know. And of course, the instructor wasn't very happy about it. They called him and told him that I was over here. So what happened, they flew -- I don't know what it was, but anyway, they flew down there with an extra, additional pilot, and one came with me, and the other one went with him, with the co-pilot, you know, that was supposed to be watching. So we got through okay. He says where are we heading for, and show me any landmarks. Do you see what, do you recognize this on the map?

And I says, yeah, and then everything went fine. So we got home and everything. We never did hear much about it. They didn't chew us out or anything. And then finally, we graduated in 45C, that's 1945. Well, what happened then, of course, we were assigned to a regular air field. Like I was assigned to, and a bunch of other guys, to Waco Air Base down there. And we did a little flying over there. We didn't do too much, being new, you know, and they didn't, you know, too much, to put too much stress on us and so on. So we flew around a little bit. We went and checked out, or I checked out another pilot that just came from overseas in a B-25, and that went fine.

And shortly after that, why we were hearing that the war was winding down, you know. This was already in '46. So, not long after that, old Uncle Sam sends everybody a letter. He says, we got too many pilots, and we have more pilots than we have airplanes. And we don't need everybody, you know. So they went, they decided that the newest pilots would be the ones that would be discharged. Well, here I was -- by the way, I graduated as a flying officer, and the other ones, the other group, some of them they graduated as second lieutenants. But I was a flight officer, which was a warrant, with a first class warrant officer, what it amounted to. Only I was, I was a pilot, ___, all the way. Anyway, we got word, and then we got the orders and everything that we were going to be discharged. And I wasn't the only one. (Phone rings.)

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Now, you graduated in 45C. So what would that be, like March of '45?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No. That happened to be more in the summer time, around June time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-hum.

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Around June, right around there. It was the middle of summer.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So you were still taking your training when VE Day came along, right, in May --

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No, my training was already over with in 45C. When we ended, when we graduated there, I was a fully qualified pilot to go ahead and go either higher or to bombers or go as a B-25 pilot. And so, yeah, then, first, like I said, we were sent to -- I forget now, I think it was Selma, or some place, Mississippi, for discharge papers and everything, and we were sent there, and I got my discharge from the Air Force sometime in '46. I think it was around April or somewhere around there. So I says, well, what do I do now, you know. They didn't need me anymore, because I was -- but when I first, you know, when the war was going on, they wouldn't let you go. But now, the war was winding down, they didn't need you. They didn't need so many pilots. So they decided to discharge about 10,000 of us. I don't know. Anyway, I was a civilian then for a while. But they did tell me this, that if you want to come back as an enlisted man, we will reenlist you as a master sergeant, which is the highest rank, just another step under warrant. If you decide you want to go back, we'll give you a rank of master sergeant, which was something, you know, instead of just going in as a buck private again. So anyway, I stayed out almost the three months, and I went to different places. I put in for tower operator in operations, which was associated with the Air Force, you know, in my line of work. I didn't try for a pilot anywhere because, hell, there was not very many airfields at that time, and furthermore, there was a surplus of pilots in the first place. So there wasn't much chance trying to get into one of those things, so I never even tried it. So I reenlisted three months later, and I got an assignment in Alamogordo, New Mexico, as an operations specialist, which is base operations which was closely related working with pilots and, you know, making up maps and routes and things like that for the pilots so that they wouldn't have to spend their time to make a set up a map from here to there, you know. I made it out for them and gave them all the information, and they just signed up and I sent it. And then it was my job to send like the flight plan to wherever they were going, you know. It was part of my work. So I did that for three years, and of course, that was during the time when they, the first atom bomb was blown up, you know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You were still in the Air Force the first time when the first bombs were dropped, right, in August of '45?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: When the experimental bomb was blown.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When they were trying the hydrogen bombs and dropping them on the islands, that sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No, that was -- this was in New Mexico in '44 -- let's see now. It was the forties -- let's see. '46, I was discharged. '47. Shortly after, it was 1947, where they, near the town of Las Cruces.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Sure. Did you witness any of those tests?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Did I what?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Witness any of those?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No, no, I didn't. In fact, I didn't even know what it was myself, because they kept it such a hush, hush, you know, thing. But I found out later that, well, how did the people that called in, you know, they were asking, what was the big boom we heard not too long ago. He say, oh, we blew up a bunch of old ammunition and old bombs and old ammunition dump that we decided we didn't need them anymore, so that was the big boom you heard. Actually, it was a small atom bomb. Then, of course, then it was made bigger and everything. That's the way, the same bomb that they used on Nagasaki, was it, and Hiroshima. Anyway, I stayed at France Field -- not France Field, Holloman Air Force Base, which was in New Mexico, and I stayed there, I guess, about four, five years. And during that time, I joined the Masons, too, you know. It just kind of interested me, talking to some of the Mason people that were there. And so I got, I went into Masons, got raised as a first degree Mason, so on and so forth. And shortly after that, I reenlisted again, and I was thinking that I was pretty well set in Holloman, I was going to stay there almost until I retired. So no, what happened was that they decided they wanted to send me to Korea. I says, okay. So I went there and spent a whole year over there, and the war was winding down down there also, you know. This was on the tail end of the Korean War. Things were getting to settle down and everything. And by the way, I never did get into the World War II, the main fighting, because my training ended as the war was ending. So I didn't get to go overseas as a combat pilot or nothing, so I kind of always was on the tail end of everything that happened, you know, major. So I stayed there a year. And while there, it was all right. I had the operations work there, of course, same as state side. And of course, while you're there, you go around, you travel around. You see what they had there, and you see the people, see how they lived, and so on and so forth. And they had a PX over there like they do over here in this country, or in the states. And I bought a lot of camera equipment, you know. Well, there was everybody you saw running around or walking around had a camera stuck around his neck. That was part of the uniform, I guess. Anyway, I bought a camera. I bought a Canon, and I paid around a hundred some dollars which would cost around 300 at that time here. And anyway, I bought all the equipment, and I still have it. And I gave it to my son. And he says, oh, that's old fashioned. We can't operate this kind of a camera any more, you know, where you have to adjust the lens opener, and lampening (ph), and the speed and all that stuff. That's too old-fashioned for him, so I guess he still got it in the case and never did take it out. But anyway, I came back and, back to Roswell. This was, now I was assigned to Roswell Air Force Base, and SAC was the main branch, Strategic Air Command and all. And they had, of course, the bombers there, the big B-52s, and I don't think they had -- I don't think they came out with the jets yet when I was there. But 52 was the biggest and -- well, it wasn't the biggest, but B-36 was the biggest plane the Air Force ever had. And I flew on those, in both of them. In fact, B-36, I went on a 90-day, more like a training, a training -- what you call it, for training purposes, in case you had to move like we did in France Field going to the jungle, you know. Well, this was moving from Roswell, New Mexico, to Guam. We flew way over to Guam and set up, set the base up there and set up everything for operations and so on.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you actually fly the B-36?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: I didn't fly it, no. I was a crew member on that one. No, that's -- I was already a master sergeant then, you know. But I was a gunner, an armament member. And I probably could have been an engineer, but they had a regular crew assigned to the plane, so they didn't want to break it up. Anyway, we flew there. Flew to Guam by way of Hawaii. We landed there, and then we fueled up and went to Guam, set up our operations and everything, and training programs. They had regular missions, training missions and one thing or another. And one time they decided, well, as a -- I guess, a more or less to show off what the United States has or what they can do, we all, all the crew piled up into the B-36 and we flew to Japan, landed over there. And those people over there, they just -- there was a big fence, you know, around the air field. You couldn't come in closer. And that thing was full everyday. Everyday that we were there, they were looking at this monster. What were we doing? How they -- you know, and everything. And it was a monster. I don't know if you ever saw one or not.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: I don't know that I ever seen one, no.

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Well, I could show you a model later. Anyway, it was a ten-engine plane, really, six crusher type engines with the props in the back and four jets, two on each tip of the wing, you know. So we stayed there for a while and looked -- whatever we were doing, we were just visiting, but the officials in that, you know, the pilot and co-pilot, they probably had some kind of conference with the Japanese, you know, people, or whatever, the embassy, you know, whatever they had there. And that was an experience, too, that I really enjoyed. And when we left, we loaded up. We went to Guam back and loaded up with fuel and everything. I mean, we loaded up to the hilt. And everybody, of course, that was there, they would buy a little something, you know, and a lot of the guys on a crew would buy them little scooters, you know, them little two wheel scooters that you see running around today, you know. They think it's something new. Well, it isn't. That's been 30 years ago they had those. Anyway, a lot of the guys bought those little scooters for two, $300 a piece, you know, something like that. So they put them on a plane and loaded everything up and here we are ready to go, leave Guam for home. Well, okay, everything was okay. We taxied out and everything else. We check the engines out and everything, and says, well, everybody ready, let's go. And we took off. And the damn thing was so loaded, it was so heavy with fuel and all the junk that the guys bought, that we just barely got off at the under of the runway, and the next step would have been the ocean, because that's where the runway ended, you know, right next to the ocean. And I said, well, wow, we're flying awful low, aren't we? He says, yeah, we're about feet above the water. I says, how come, you know. And of course, they told me, well, they got to fly off some of the fuel so that they can climb up to altitude. I says, oh, okay. I guess we were really loaded, I guess lucky to get off the ground. And of course, it took us -- we didn't stop at Hawaii this time. We just flew directly from Guam to Roswell. No fuel, no refueling or nothing, you know. So that had a long range. And he says that, they found later that it could have gone as far as Chicago, you know, one long range, you know, flight. So we landed at Roswell and everything, and we got home safe and got loaded and got set up again. And as time went on, why I stayed there about, I think I was there six or seven years, six years or so before I retired, and I retired there at Roswell as a master sergeant. And those three guys standing up there with me are the base commander and my squadron commander, and I'm in the middle getting my discharge. And that's when I was, that was the end of my military career. And ever since that time, I was on the reserve, what they call. So I put in my ten years in the reserves, gave me a total of 30 years, and I got a notice from the Air Force Department that I would be elevated to the highest rank that I held, which was the warrant. So, I think I have some copies here. And so I was retired as a warrant officer and -- until today. Still getting there. I have a lot of copies of these. You can have this if you want. They're all the same.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: These are all the same?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: So, so I've been retired now since 19 -- let's see, 40, 20, 60, 20 years active, and ten years reserve. So 1970, I've been retired, so I've been receiving a check from Uncle Sam all this time. Oh, here's an order here. Here's an order here that says when, at the end of my training. See the date is June 27th.

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So do you remember any wild celebrations when the war came to an end, where you were?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No, not in -- the base I was at, I was discharged, and I was then in Alamogordo. No, there wasn't what you might say a lot of celebration going on. They were too busy experimenting with missiles and they were too busy experimenting with all kinds of stuff there, like the bomb. They were probably busy putting that together, you know. So they didn't pay too much attention to it. They knew what was going on anyway, you know. So, that was it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you think when you heard the news about them dropping the first atomic bomb on Japan?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Well, a lot of people seemed to think that it was unnecessary, but I think it was, that it saved a lot of lives. It killed a lot of lives, it took a lot of, you know, civilian people, but it did shorten the war. Because I think we would have to be really, I mean, the force that would be, have to be three times as big as what it was to try and invade and take that island of Japan. I don't think that we would, we would probably lose thousands and thousands of people, airmen and soldiers and, of course, Japanese, too, before this was, before they were conquered. So this, they say, was -- some of them say it shortened the war, and some of them say it wasn't necessary. So I guess you have to draw your own conclusion on that. But Japan, the fanatics that they were at that time -- well, they still are, I guess, when it comes to fighting for their country, so they would probably die first before they, you know, they would walk into a machine gun, and you just shoot them right down, you know. That's how they were. Actually, I believe the big belief at that time was that they would -- well, they still do. If you get killed fighting for your country that you go right straight to heaven. There is no detours or nothing anywhere. You just go straight up. Well, that's fine, I mean, you know, that relief, but you are still just as dead as if you didn't, you know. So I think that it was, it ended the war sooner than it would have. It probably would have gone another three or four years or maybe who knows how long. So I kind of felt that, well, it kind of paid back a little bit for what they did to Hawaii, and it made them decide that they better not fight anymore if we have this bomb, they'll just drop some more of them and eliminate Japan, you might say. So that was the end as far as my thinking about it, is that it was good in one way, and it was, you know, kind of harsh on the civilian population that were involved in it, so, so I don't know.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news when FDR died?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: I heard the news, but I didn't hear anything special.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: The reaction around you wasn't anything out of the ordinary?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: In the military, those kind of actions or activities didn't bother us because we were involved in it involuntarily all the time. Like the president, well, he was the commander-in-chief of the Air Force, the Army, and all that, and we were more or less informed of what was going on, and then when it actually did happen, the civilian population didn't know anything about it, but we kind of had a hunch, you know, what was going on in military circles, you know. In other words, you're living in a different world when you're in --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It wasn't like we've seen the scenes of the civilian population having this great sadness when FDR died, it wasn't that way in the military?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Not to any great extent.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you get much entertainment during your time in the service?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What did you do for relaxation when you got a break?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: Well, my break was, when I was in Roswell, I went ahead and put in for night manager in the NCO Club, and there was an NCO in charge of it, it was the top man, or top, you know, that was running the place, and then he could use -- I put in for an assistant manager to run the club at the, in the evening, you know, from four until nine or ten or whatever time we closed. Now, that was my entertainment. That was my relaxation. I would go there and talk to people, and we had dances, and we had, you know, different things like NCO club does. And they celebrated different holidays. That was my relaxation, because I celebrated with them. I was right there. So as far as me being, having, going out with the groups while I was on duty and go celebrate, no, I never did. I never did go like that, you know. The only thing I ever did do was when I was down in Alamogordo is during the hunting season, I would take a 30-day leave, you know, and I would get together with the other GIs, other sold ers, and we would go up into the hills around Alamogordo and do some deer hunting. That's about all, really, that's about all that I would do that was different than actual duties, you know, what I was supposed to do, you know, in the service. So you know, I wasn't what you call a party man, no.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: When you think about your time in the service in the Air Force, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: You mean active-wise or --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: -- being involved in an action or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yeah, whatever, when you think about that time, whatever comes --

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: No, I was not -- I didn't -- like I said, I was always getting in on the tail end of everything. The Second World War was dying down or turning down, and then there was ended, and of course, when I went to Korea, that thing was dying down, didn't have much action there. So actually, the highest point of my military life would be graduating as a pilot in the Air Force. That, I can say, is the only thing that really worthwhile that, you know, I got out of the service, I learned out to fly a damn airplane. Yeah, I understand that at that particular time, too, that the government would spend training one person from beginning to end $250,000 for a man. Now, you figure in my class, my class was, I think around maybe 20, and then you got to figure how many classes followed or before that, the government spent millions and millions of dollars on training pilots. And then they say I don't need you, we're all finished with you, good bye, like water going under the bridge, you know. And you know what got me, mostly, got me kind of teed off was I found out that as we were being discharged, there were new classes following us that they were, they're still training more pilots, more classes. Now, why didn't they stop that program and say we don't need you anymore, we don't need to train you anymore. They didn't. They kept having more classes one right after the other. So I just couldn't figure that out, you know. I still can't figure it out why they would kick out a qualified pilot and keep training more new ones, you know. That didn't make sense to me at that time. But then I found out later that they have so much money allotted to each branch, say billions of dollars. And if they don't spend the billions of dollars, then the next allotment or the next thing that they're going to be asking for, they won't get it, or they'll get less than what they're asking for. They'll get less than what they're asking for anyway. You know, if they're asking for 2,000,000,000, they may get a billion-and-a-half. So that's why they always ask for more, because they knew they weren't going to get it. So that's the same game they're playing today. Well, those days are gone, and the only thing I would have to say is this, that the young people today that don't know what they want to do with themselves, don't know which way they're heading, they don't know what they want to get into as professionally, I think it would be a good deal, a good thing for them to just say, well, pick the branch of service that they would like the most. Like if you want to be a sailor, go in the Navy. If you want to be a marine, go to the Marines, army, Army. Each one of those branchs has their elite, I don't know, I guess what you would call segments, let's say, like the Army has the Airborne, the Navy has the Seals. Air Force, of course, they don't have nothing. They're just Air Force. But anyway -- I don't know if the Air Force has any special training units that I know of.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They must, but I don't know.

sp.speaker: Charles Ginza
sp.p: They probably do. It probably has to do with Airborne, similar to the Army Airborne. That's what my son went into in the Army. He, out of high school, he went into the Army, and he wanted to be an Airborne parachutist, which he was a parachutist, but then somehow he got into Airborne, it was heavy artillery, connected with heavy artillery where they would drop these cannons, these tanks, and whatever, you know. And then he would parachute down, and they would be there ready to, you know, get back into, right away into action.

Anyway, I think that would be a good deal for a young guy today. It's only three years, and it would be an experience that he will never forget. And he may find what he wants to do, because today, every service, branch of service you hear about, you can get into computers, you can get into doctors, you can become anything that you want, you know, as far as a high paying profession. And today even, they will send you through doctor's, you know, school, colleges and all that, but you have to pay back the government them two years or three years out of the service to pay back the loan that you got, you might say, or the training that you got, which a lot of them do.

A lot of them will go ahead and become a doctor and then put three years in at Fort Slocum, or air field, or some air field or branch of service, you know, in Korea or Japan. But he has to pay back the two years or three years that the government was sending him for school, to learn. So then a lot of them stay and a lot of them get out and become professional doctors, you know, in civilian life. But I think that it would be, it wouldn't hurt anybody to put in two or three years into a service and pick what you want and not -- as a rule today, you get what you want. In my time, they didn't. I wanted to be a machinist. I like machine shop work. I never even saw a machine shop in the Air Force. My machine shop was at the end of the broom handle, you know, sweeping up the hangar floor. No, I think it would be a good, good training, and it wouldn't hurt the guy, and another thing, while he's looking around and looking for something to do, he may get in with the wrong crowd and then he gets into dope or get into, you know -- well, you never know what, anything to just to be doing something. And this way, he would have something to do. You know, he would have something to look forward to. He had to do something. He had this to do.

And if you wanted to be promoted, you had to show that you're qualified. You had to take a test and everything. I mean, you could always get promoted, you know, go further. But today, the kids today though, they, heck, the Navy or the Army, why that's the farthest thing from their mind. But if the war would break out tomorrow, who do you think would go in? Draft you. (Noises.) You would be getting them like what, just pick them up, say you're drafted, and we're going to make a soldier out of you, or whatever. And then that's what they would do. Actually, when they do draft you, they don't draft you for the Air Force. They draft you for doughboy, the guy that's going to be out in the mud or out in the field with a rifle.

So I don't know, this -- everything is so changed today, you know, so highly technical, you would be surprised. My son spent 20 years in the Army in the Airborne. He's out near Fort Bragg now. And he's discharged with years. And he was an armorer, tank, heavy artillery man, you know. And you look into the tank, he had a dashboard that looked like it was in an aircraft, like an airplane dashboard. I say, what are all these instruments for, you know. They were getting all so, so what you might say, so far advanced that everything, they can just aim the gun, and they don't even have to see it. They watch this instrument, you know, and it tells them, oh, cripe, it's all sophisticated, you know. Oh, well.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
